## reference · error-message-quality-guidelines
* Display error messages close to the error's source to reduce cognitive load.
* Use noticeable, redundant, and accessible indicators such as bold, high-contrast, and red text.
* Design errors based on their impact, using different formats for minor and severe errors.
* Avoid prematurely displaying errors, and consider inline, real-time errors for error-prone interactions.
* Use human-readable language, avoiding technical jargon and obscure error codes.
* Concisely and precisely describe the issue, providing context and potential remedies.
* Offer constructive advice and take a positive tone, avoiding blame and humor.
* Safeguard against likely mistakes, preserving the user's input and reducing error-correction effort.
* Concisely educate users on how the system works and how to resolve errors.
* Mitigate total failure with novelty, using surprising or entertaining content to salvage disappointing situations.
* Use proximity to help users associate error messages with the relevant interface elements.
* Leverage carefully designed animations to guide the user's visual attention for corrections.
* Consider the roughly 350 million people worldwide with a color-vision deficiency when designing error messages.
* Use modal dialogs for severe errors that require the user's attention and resolution.
* Conditionally displayed labels, toast notifications, or banners can be used for issues needing minimal user interaction.
* Avoid using exclusively color or animation to indicate errors.
* Provide details of when a product will be available again or suggest alternatives for out-of-stock items.
* Include instructions on how to resolve an error, using hypertext for additional information.
* Explain how the system works and how to avoid similar errors in the future.
Sources: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/error-message-guidelines/
